open-question.question: The milestones tool's new `since` query finds a milestone's anchor, its latest `Starting-state:` commit, by subject and by the milestone's `requirements.md` path. Nothing is added for a live milestone the migration kept in place: it reads as having no starting state until a `Starting-state:` commit under its path lands. Matches how the tool already reads finish commits (only the path-form `Milestone-finish: <path>` subject counts, the id form never read), so the anchor rule is the one subject the workflow now writes, needs no legacy branch, and cannot take a hand-typed or stray `Starting-state:` subject as the anchor. The affected set is small and shrinks on its own: in this repository all 44 bare-name `Starting-state:` commits belong to finished milestones and both live milestones carry the path form, so only a migrated project's milestone that stayed live is affected, and only until it is finished or its starting state is recorded again under its path. A migrated project's live milestone whose starting state was recorded under the bare-name subject gets an empty `since` print, the "no starting state has been written" outcome, although its section is filled. The skill then runs a first run over a filled section, and the task-entry writers meet the no-anchor case, whose handling the sibling question on a missing anchor at task entry owns, so this option is only as harmless as that outcome makes it.

The anchor is the latest commit whose subject opens with `Starting-state:`, whatever follows the marker, among the commits that changed `<path>requirements.md`. The milestone is identified by the path-scoped file filter alone, as `tasks` selects every `Task-completion:` subject and identifies the milestone by the file list rather than by the subject's descriptor, so the bare-name subject an earlier release wrote is found the same way as the path form. A live milestone kept in place by `/migrate-milestones` keeps its recorded starting state as its anchor, so its first `since` call reads a refresh or a no-op rather than a first run, and the rule is one prefix test with no legacy form named in the tool: the commit tool scopes every `Starting-state:` commit to its own milestone's files, so the path filter already tells milestones apart, including two scopes holding one slug, whose bare names would collide. Any commit that changed the file under a `Starting-state:` subject counts, a hand-made one with a free descriptor included, so the anchor rule is looser than the path-form rule the finish read uses, and the tool reads two subject families by two different rules (`Milestone-finish:` by its exact path, `Starting-state:` by prefix), which the help text and the invariant have to state and justify.

The anchor is the latest commit, among those that changed `<path>requirements.md`, whose subject is exactly `Starting-state: <path>` or exactly `Starting-state: <name>`, `<name>` being the milestone directory's last path component, the bare-name form earlier releases wrote. A subject under any other descriptor is not read, and the help text names the two accepted forms. Finds every starting state either the current or an earlier release recorded, so a migrated live milestone keeps its anchor, while still refusing a stray or hand-typed `Starting-state:` subject whose descriptor names neither form; both forms are exact tests derived from the path the tool is given, with the file filter keeping a bare name that two scopes share from matching across them. Writes a legacy subject form into the tool permanently, a second accepted spelling with its own test fixtures and help-text sentence, kept for a population that only shrinks (migrated milestones that stayed live) and that the other history queries deliberately do not serve, since the finish read accepts the path form alone.

open-question.question: In a shallow clone the truncated log can omit a milestone's `Starting-state:` commit, so the new `since` query would read a recorded starting state as never written. Does `since` refuse a shallow repository as `gate` does, or read whatever the log yields with the limit stated only in its help text, as the history queries do?
open-question.alternative: `since` runs the same `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` test `gate` runs (the existing `is_shallow()` helper), before any log read and in both forms, the broad one and `--milestones`, and refuses on `true` with one `Error:` line naming `git fetch --unshallow` as the remedy, whatever the truncated log would have yielded. Its help text and the milestones-tool invariant then name two queries that check, `gate` and `since`, in place of "only `gate`". `since` is the starting-state procedure's opening call, so one refusal there stops the whole procedure before anything is read: a shallow clone can then neither report a recorded starting state as never written nor go on to the later `milestones` and `summary` reads, which the same truncated log would also make silently incomplete, and write a section grounded in a partial record. The case costs nothing at the task-entry writers, which check `gate` first and so already stop in a shallow clone before `since --milestones` runs; the check reuses a helper and a message the tool already has. It also refuses the shallow clones where the answer would have been right, any clone deep enough to hold the anchor, so `specify-milestone-starting-state` cannot run at all in a shallow checkout (a CI-style `--depth` clone, for instance) until it is unshallowed, and it widens a rule the third milestone settled as `gate` alone checking. What the skill does with the `Error:` line (a fixed stop line, or going on without the read) is the "Starting-state read failure" question's to settle.

`since` reads the log first and runs the shallow test only when it found no `Starting-state:` anchor for the milestone's `requirements.md`, refusing then with the same `Error:` line and `git fetch --unshallow` remedy; when the anchor was found it prints its lines as usual in a shallow clone and a complete one alike. The refusal applies to both forms, and the help text states that a shallow clone is refused only where the missing anchor might be truncation. It refuses exactly the one output the question names as wrong: a found anchor and every commit after it are newer than the anchor and so present in the truncated log, which makes those lines trustworthy, while "no line" is the only answer a shallow clone can falsify. A shallow clone deep enough to hold the anchor keeps working, and nothing is refused that would have been read correctly by `since` itself. The query's behaviour now depends on what it found as well as on the repository, a second code path and a refusal rule harder to state in one help-text sentence than either uniform form, and the protection ends at `since`: on a found anchor the procedure goes on to the `milestones` and `summary` reads, which the truncated log can still leave incomplete with no sign, so a refresh in a shallow clone may still miss older milestones. What the skill does on the refusal is the "Starting-state read failure" question's to settle.

`since` gets no shallow check: it prints whatever the truncated path-scoped log yields, with no stop line and no warning, exactly as `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, and `record` do, and its help text and the docs state the limit (a shallow clone can omit the anchor, which then reads as no starting state written). `gate` stays the one query that checks, and the invariant's "only `gate`" stands unchanged. It keeps the tool's settled split, `gate` alone checking because a gate passing silently lets two runs collide while a history reader wants what is there, and adds no code, no refusal, and no failure for any runner to handle. The missed anchor is mild in effect: the task-entry writers never reach `since` in a shallow clone because `gate` refuses first, and in `specify-milestone-starting-state` a missed anchor only turns a refresh or a no-op into a first run, which edits the section in place, leaving byte-identical every subsection whose facts still hold, and lands a new `Starting-state:` commit that becomes the anchor from then on. In a shallow clone the skill misreads a recorded starting state as never written with no sign to anyone, pays an exploration the no-op line would have spared, and may write prose for unchanged facts that the next review pass reads as change; the later record reads it explores with are truncated just as silently, so the refreshed section can be grounded in a partial history and nothing tells the operator to unshallow.

open-question.question: The starting-state procedure reads `live` filtered to its milestone's scope and the `milestones` overview on that scope, and the review pass reads the same overview, but each runner holds only the milestone's path (`<scope>/milestones/<slug>/`). Both queries keep one PATH argument, `live` gaining it as optional: the tool reads a PATH naming a directory directly inside a `milestones/` container, by `gate`'s lexical test, as that milestone and filters on its scope, and reads any other PATH as a directory, as `milestones PATH` does today. open-question.question: A refresh that explores and finds nothing to change in the `## Relevant starting state` section lands no commit, so the anchor stays where it was and every later run in the same stale window (the skill run again, or the next `derive-tasks` or `submit-task` entry) explores again. The runner records each unchanged exploration outside the tracked tree, in a per-clone file (under `.git/` or an ignored path) holding the milestone's path and the newest commit the `since` print listed, and the procedure skips exploring when that print's newest commit matches the recorded one. Commits, the anchor rule, the commit tool, and `requirements.md` stay unchanged. It bounds the repeat at one exploration per change in the ground per clone while leaving the log, the anchor's meaning, the commit tool's no-op contract, and the section's prose exactly as they are. It brings back stored state outside git of the kind the project rejected for a current milestone: it is per clone and invisible to a reviewer, lost on a fresh clone and absent on another machine, and it needs a writer the plugin does not have, since the milestones tool writes nothing and no document writer touches anything but its own document. A stale or hand-copied cache would make a runner skip an exploration silently.

open-question.question: The starting-state procedure opens with the milestones tool's `since` query and then reads the record and what is in flight through `milestones`, `summary`, `show`, and `live`. When one of those calls fails (the tool refuses, or git is unavailable), what does each of the procedure's three runners (`specify-milestone-starting-state`, `derive-tasks`, `submit-task`) do: stop on a fixed line with nothing written, or go on without that read?

During a refresh the starting-state procedure clears the standing picks the changed facts undermine with one `strip --recommendation` call, made after the section has been edited. When that call fails, does the runner stop with the edit left uncommitted, as `modify-milestone-goal` does on its own failed clearing call, or commit the refreshed section with the picks left standing; and does the same hold inside `derive-tasks` and `submit-task`, where a stale state is meant never to stop the writer?

`derive-tasks` and `submit-task` are to refresh the starting state when `since --milestones` prints a line beyond the anchor line. When it prints nothing at all, because the milestone has no `Starting-state:` commit (the step was skipped, or the section was written by hand or arrived in the milestone's first commit), does the writer follow the starting-state procedure as a first run and commit it, or go on to its own write with the section as it stands?

`derive-tasks` and `submit-task` check the scope gate directly ahead of their write call today, after their reads and their authoring. The staleness check has to follow the gate and precede those reads, which moves the gate to the front of each writer. Is the gate then checked once, at the front, or again directly before the write call as well, now that the reads, a possible refresh, and the authoring stand between the check and the write?

The review pass is to read the `milestones` overview on its milestone's scope, bounded to the recent milestones, on every pass, but the `milestones` query takes no bound today and prints every milestone that ever touched the scope (56 lines on this repository's root). How is that overview bounded to the recent ones?
open-question.alternative: The bound is a count, applied in the tool: `milestones` gains an optional flag (for example `--last N`) that keeps every live line and only the N newest finished lines, by finish timestamp, the order the query already sorts them in. The review pass's one fixed call writes N as a literal (on the order of ten). Without the flag the query prints what it prints today, so `record`, `/release-plugin`, and every other reader are unchanged. The overview's size is fixed whatever the project's age or pace, so a pass repeated until convergence pays the same small print every time. It is the simplest rule to state, test on a temporary repository, and read, and it needs nothing from the starting state's anchor or from the clock. N is arbitrary and blind to the milestone: on a busy scope a milestone finished just before the starting state was written can already have fallen off, and on a quiet one the N lines reach back years past anything relevant. It adds a flag to a query whose contract the CLAUDE.md invariant spells out, so that invariant and the help text change with it.

The bound is a time window, applied in the tool: `milestones` gains an optional flag (for example `--within DAYS`) that keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit's author date falls within that many days of today. The review pass's fixed call writes the day count as a literal. "Recent" is read in its plain sense, as calendar time, so a burst of finishes all shows and a long-quiet scope prints only its live lines, and the window needs no milestone-specific anchor or count tuned to the project's milestone size. The print depends on the clock and the project's pace rather than on the milestone: a milestone that sits deciding for longer than the window loses sight of what finished just before its starting state, a dormant project sees nothing at all, and a fast one can print as much as the unbounded query. The tool's tests must pin "today", which none of its queries does now.

The bound is relative to the milestone itself, applied in the tool: the query (by a flag on `milestones`, given the milestone's path) keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit is newer than the milestone's own latest `Starting-state:` commit, the anchor the new `since` query finds, falling back to the unbounded list when the milestone has no anchor yet. On a fresh or freshly refreshed state the finished part is usually empty. It prints exactly the complement of what the starting state already carries, the milestones finished since it was written, on a branch merged in the meantime included, so the overview never repeats the starting state and stays near empty on every pass of a loop whose ground has not moved. It reuses the anchor lookup `since` needs anyway. A milestone finished before the anchor that the starting-state read did not weigh, the third case the draft gives the overview for, is never shown, so the pass relies wholly on the starting state's judgment for everything older. It needs the milestone's path rather than a scope, a condition on the scope-argument question, and inherits whatever the anchor-subject question settles about which `Starting-state:` commits count.

The bound is relative to the milestone itself, applied in the tool: the query (by a flag on `milestones`, given the milestone's path) keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit is newer than the milestone's own `Milestone-definition:` commit, a point that never moves once the milestone exists. The window is stable for the milestone's whole life and needs no starting-state anchor, so it is independent of how the `since` anchor is matched and of whether a refresh ran, and it still shows everything that finished while this milestone was being prepared. After a refresh it keeps listing milestones the refreshed starting state has already absorbed, so the overview grows with the milestone's age rather than with what is new; like the anchor form it hides older milestones the starting state did not weigh. A live milestone kept in place by the migration may carry a definition subject naming a bare directory rather than its path, so the tool needs a rule for finding it, and it takes the milestone's path, a condition on the scope-argument question.

The bound combines the milestone-relative and count forms, applied in the tool: the query keeps every live line and the finished milestones that are either newer than the milestone's latest `Starting-state:` commit or among the N newest finished ones, whichever set is larger, N written as a literal in the review pass's fixed call. It shows everything new since the starting state however many that is, and still keeps a short tail of the most recent older milestones in view, so the case of a recently finished milestone the starting-state read did not weigh is covered as well as the post-anchor one. It is the most complex rule to state, test, and explain, two bounds and a union where one would do, and it still hides anything older than the tail. It shares the anchor form's dependence on the milestone's path and on how the anchor subject is matched, both questions owned by siblings.

The bound is a count applied in the runner, not the tool: the review pass's fixed call pipes the unchanged `milestones` query on its scope through `head -n N`, N a literal, so the first N lines, the live ones first and then the newest finished, are what the pass reads. The tool and its contract do not change. No tool change, no new flag, no new tests or invariant text for the milestones tool: the bound is one fixed literal in one skill file, trivially adjusted later. Live lines eat the count, so a scope with many live milestones shows fewer finished ones; and the pipe's exit status is `head`'s, so a refused or failed tool call reads as success with an empty or partial overview unless the call adds `pipefail` or a separate test, which bears on the read-failure question. A shell filter on tool output is the kind of per-site hand-rolled step the tools exist to replace.

The premise that the overview is bounded is rejected: the review pass's fixed call reads the unchanged `milestones` query on its scope whole, every live and every finished milestone that touched it, one line each (56 lines, about 5 KB, on this repository's root today), and the pass's own judgment picks which lines bear. Nothing is ever hidden, the older milestone the starting state did not weigh included, and no tool change, flag, or bound value has to be chosen, tested, or later re-tuned; it is the query exactly as `/release-plugin` and `record` already rely on. The print grows by one line per milestone forever and is paid again on every pass of a loop that runs until convergence, the cost the draft bounds the overview to avoid; on a root-scoped project every milestone the project ever finished is listed, most of them irrelevant, which dilutes the pass's attention.

open-question.question: The review pass gains one fixed call to the milestones tool at its inventory step, the `milestones` overview. When that call fails (the tool refuses, or git is unavailable), does the pass stop on a fixed line of its own before changing anything, or report the failure and carry on reviewing from the milestone's two documents alone?
open-question.alternative: A failed overview call (any non-zero exit, the tool's `Error:` line or git's failure alike, treated as one condition and never classified by its wording) stops the pass at its inventory step, before any prune, dedup, new block, or note deletion. The pass prints one new fixed, identifier-free stop line of its own as its report's first line with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim beneath it. It makes no commit and prints neither the still-open list nor the convergence verdict. The new line gets its row in the `## Fixed console lines` table. A harness looping the review until the verdict line sees a stop, not a convergence formed without the record, and the overview stays as unconditional as the design meant ("whether to look is never the pass's choice"). It follows the precedent of the other fixed history reads in skills that write and commit: `finish-milestone` and `derive-tasks` stop on their own line when `tasks` or `list` fails. Stopping costs almost nothing extra in practice. On a scope directory that exists, `milestones PATH` refuses only when git cannot be run or its output cannot be read, and in that case the pass's own step-5 commit through the commit tool would fail too. Stopping first avoids leaving a reshaped `open_questions.xml` uncommitted behind a failed commit. It adds a stop line, a table row, and a review stop that every chain's harness must recognise. Any failure of a read that only feeds the pass's judgment blocks the requirements loop entirely, even though the two documents alone would still let the pass reconcile and surface most gaps. The same holds for a refusal introduced by a later change to the call's arguments (the bound is a sibling's to set): it stops every pass on every milestone until fixed.

A failed overview call does not stop the pass. It goes on through reconciliation, gap surfacing, the decision consistency check, and its commit, using `requirements.md` and `open_questions.xml` alone. Its report keeps its usual fixed first line (`Requirements reviewed.` or the no-op line). Below that line it adds one advisory saying the milestones overview could not be read, with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim, beside the still-open list. The convergence verdict is printed exactly as today, whenever the closing `list` prints nothing. No new fixed line is added. The loop engine keeps doing its core job on a read that only complements the starting state, which is how the conversational readers treat a failed history read (`ask-in-milestone-context` tells it in prose and carries on). The fixed-lines table, the verdict's contract, and every chain's expected lines stay unchanged. A harness matching the verdict leaves the loop on a pass that never saw the record. The overview exists to catch exactly one case, a milestone finished since the starting state or merged in from a branch, and that case then reaches task derivation unflagged, with the advisory visible only to a human reading the message. It also adds a new advisory kind to the short list of decision-critical advisories. When git itself is the failure, the pass carries on only to fail at its step-5 commit, leaving its edits uncommitted.

A failed overview call does not stop the pass. It reconciles, surfaces gaps, checks decisions against each other, and commits from the two documents alone, keeping its usual fixed first line and adding one advisory below it with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim. On such a pass the convergence verdict line is never printed, even when the closing `list` prints nothing, and the still-open list is reported as usual. The pass still does all the reshaping work the two documents allow. A harness looping until the verdict does not take a review that skipped the record for a converged one, so a degraded pass can never send the milestone on to task derivation. The verdict now carries a second condition, which breaks its listed contract of being printed whenever `list` prints nothing. Its documentation and its fixed-lines test semantics would have to change. A loop whose overview keeps failing re-runs the review until the harness's own cap, never converging and never showing a stop line that names why. When git itself is the failure, the step-5 commit fails anyway.

open-question.question: Each of the three chains on the ways-of-using page that derive and complete tasks ("Answering the questions that matter to you", "Putting more intelligence into a stuck milestone", "Executing tasks") is to open with the refresh line and one review pass. A question that review raises needs an alternatives line, a recommend line, and an answer line before `derive-tasks` will run, and two of the three chains carry no alternatives line today. What lines does each of those chains carry between its opening review and its derivation line?

The benchmark draft's two cairn deliveries each run one unbroken chain per phase: the starting-state line, the bounded review loop, then the derivation line directly behind the loop. Once every execution chain on the ways-of-using page opens with the refresh line and a review pass, do the benchmark deliveries gain a second starting-state line ahead of their derivation line, or keep the one they have?

The host-suite test needs `derive-tasks` to find its milestone's scope free and its starting state stale, which takes a second, overlapping milestone whose task or finish commits land after the first milestone's `Starting-state:` commit and which no longer holds the scope when `derive-tasks` runs. Is that second milestone seeded as already finished in the seeded repository's history, or left live in the seed and finished through the host by the test before it derives?

The new host-suite test is to assert the refresh on all three hosts, but the suite runs on demand, outside CI, and can pass on a host only after the rebuilt tree is committed and that host's installed plugin copy is refreshed by hand. Does completing this milestone require a passing run of the test against each of the three hosts, the task that runs it refreshing the installed copies first, or only that the test is delivered and passes on the hosts available when it lands?
open-question.alternative: Completion requires a passing run of the whole host suite, the new test included, against each of the three hosts (`--host claude`, `--host antigravity`, `--host codex`). The task that runs it starts, once the rebuilt tree is committed, by refreshing each host's installed copy on the maintainer's machine with that host's documented install, as the host-generic suite milestone's "Refreshing installed copies" decision has its suite-running tasks do. A host that fails is fixed inside this milestone before it finishes. It verifies the goal's "on all three hosts" claim before the milestone closes and meets the rule CONTRIBUTING.md already sets, that a change under `host_tests/` owes a passing run on all three hosts before it is committed, following the precedent the sibling suite milestone recorded. The milestone cannot finish without all three CLIs installed and working on the maintainer's machine, up to three 20-minute headless runs, and a task runner writing into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn`, `~/.codex/plugins/cache/`, and Claude Code's plugin install, which may prompt for permission or fail in an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run. A host integration defect the new test exposes becomes this milestone's work and holds its finish.

Completion requires a passing run against each of the three hosts, as above, but no task refreshes an installed copy: the maintainer brings each copy up to date by hand outside the task run, and the task that runs the suite stops with its tree left resumable on the suite's `host suite prerequisite missing:` line for any host whose copy is stale, to be resumed once the copy is refreshed. A host that fails is fixed inside this milestone. It keeps the full three-host verification while no agent run of this workflow writes to any installation outside the repository, extending the suite's own no-write-to-installations rule to the runner that drives it. The task that runs the suite cannot complete in one unattended pass: it needs a human step between the rebuilt tree's commit and the run, so a headless chain stops there and the milestone waits on the maintainer, and it carries the same CLI-availability and host-defect costs as the task-refresh form.

Completion requires that the test is delivered and passes on each host whose CLI is installed on the maintainer's machine when the task runs. The task refreshes those hosts' installed copies first, and a host whose CLI is absent is not run, its run left to the release pre-flight's check g, which selects all three hosts because `host_tests/` changed. A host that is run and fails is fixed inside this milestone. A missing CLI on the maintainer's machine never blocks the milestone, while every host that can be run is still verified before finish. It falls short of CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule for a `host_tests/` change, and the goal's three-host claim may stand unverified on a host until the next release, where a failure found by check g stops the release outside any milestone.

Completion requires that the test is delivered and passes on each host whose installed copy already matches the committed built tree when the task runs, with no installed copy refreshed by the task or required of the maintainer. In practice that is the Claude Code install reading from the checkout's `hosts/claude/` through the directory marketplace, whose freshness check passes trivially; every other host is left to the release pre-flight's check g. It needs no write to any installation and no human step, so the task completes unattended while still running the new test end to end on at least the host that loads straight from the checkout. It verifies at most one host before finish, falling short of both the goal's three-host assertion and CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule, and leaves Antigravity and Codex behaviour, the hosts whose integrations most often differed, to be discovered at release.

The task refreshes all three installed copies and runs the suite against each host, but completion requires only that the three runs are made and their outcomes recorded, not that every one passes: a host failing for a defect in that host's integration rather than in this milestone's refresh behaviour is recorded as a follow-up (a task submitted to a later milestone, or a note in that host's `settings.toml` hands-on block) and does not hold the finish, while a failure of the refresh behaviour itself is fixed here. Every host is exercised before finish and nothing is left undiscovered, while a host-specific integration defect unrelated to the starting-state refresh cannot keep this milestone from closing. It ships a test known to fail on a host, so `main` would fail CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule for that host and the next release's check g until the follow-up lands, and telling a host integration defect from a refresh defect is a judgment made at run time with no fixed test.

Completion requires only that the test is written and committed with the rebuilt trees, with no host run as part of the milestone and no installed copy refreshed by it. Its first runs are the release pre-flight's check g, which selects all three hosts because `host_tests/` changed since the last release, and any failure there is handled outside this milestone. The milestone completes entirely from the repository and the automated tool tests, with no external CLI, no write to any installation, and no 20-minute headless runs, while the release gate already guarantees the test runs on all three hosts before anything ships. The test's correctness is unproven when the milestone finishes, it breaks CONTRIBUTING.md's rule that a `host_tests/` change owes a passing run on all three hosts before it is committed, and a fault in the test or in the refresh it asserts surfaces at release time, after the milestone's directory and context are gone.
